title: Gut Tube, Vessels & Visceral Nerves
summary: Follow the midgut and hindgut and master the arterial, portal venous and autonomic supply of the whole gut.

lessons.title: Jejunum, Ileum and the Mesentery

levels.kid:
Your small intestine is a long, soft tube that is folded up inside your belly like a garden hose. It is where most of your food gets soaked up into your blood.

It has three parts. The first short part is the duodenum. The next part is the **jejunum**. It is wide, red and busy, like a crowded kitchen. The last part is the **ileum**. It is thinner and paler, and it soaks up special things like vitamin B12.

The tube is not loose. It hangs from a fan-shaped sheet called the **mesentery**. The fan holds the tube in place, like a curtain holds onto its rod. Tiny blood vessels run through the fan to feed the tube, so it can move and still stay safe.
levels.hs:
The **small intestine** runs from the stomach to the large intestine. In a living adult it is roughly 3 to 6 meters long, and it has three parts: the **duodenum** (about 25 cm), the **jejunum** (about two-fifths of the rest) and the **ileum** (about three-fifths). This lesson covers the jejunum and ileum.

The jejunum begins at the **duodenojejunal flexure**, a bend held up by the **suspensory muscle of the duodenum** (ligament of Treitz). The ileum ends at the **ileocecal junction**, where it joins the cecum in the lower right abdomen.

How to tell them apart:
- **Jejunum**: wider, thicker wall, deeper red, lots of tall inner folds (**plicae circulares**), mostly upper left abdomen.
- **Ileum**: narrower, thinner, paler, fewer folds, more fat in its mesentery, and patches of immune tissue called **Peyer's patches**. Mostly lower right abdomen and pelvis.

Both hang from the **mesentery**, a double fold of peritoneum (the thin lining of the abdomen). Its root is only about 15 cm long, but its free edge fans out to hold several meters of gut. Arteries, veins, lymph vessels and nerves travel between its two layers.

Real example: the terminal ileum absorbs **vitamin B12** and bile salts. People who have had it removed for **Crohn's disease** may need B12 replaced by injection for life.
levels.college:
**Position and boundaries.** The jejunum and ileum are intraperitoneal and mobile, lying in the infracolic compartment framed by the colon. The jejunum starts at the **duodenojejunal flexure** at about the level of L2, to the left of the midline, suspended by the **suspensory muscle of the duodenum (Treitz)**. The ileum ends at the **ileocecal junction** in the right iliac fossa. There is no sharp border between them; the change is gradual.

**The mesentery.** The **root of the mesentery** is about 15 cm long and runs obliquely from the DJ flexure down to the right sacroiliac joint. It crosses, in order: the third part of the duodenum, the abdominal aorta, the IVC, the right ureter and the right psoas major. Between its two peritoneal layers it carries:
- **Superior mesenteric artery (SMA)** branches and **superior mesenteric vein (SMV)** tributaries
- Lymphatics and roughly 100 to 200 **mesenteric lymph nodes**, which drain to superior mesenteric nodes
- Autonomic fibers running with the arteries on the superior mesenteric plexus
- Variable amounts of fat

**Distinguishing features (a classic exam table, in words):**
- **Diameter and wall**: jejunum about 2 to 4 cm, thick; ileum about 2 to 3 cm, thin.
- **Color**: jejunum deep red (more vascular); ileum paler pink.
- **Vasa recta**: long and straight in the jejunum; short in the ileum.
- **Arterial arcades**: one or two large loops in the jejunum; many tiers of smaller loops in the ileum.
- **Mesenteric fat**: less in the jejunum, so you can see "windows" near the gut wall; more in the ileum, reaching up to the wall.
- **Plicae circulares**: tall and dense in the jejunum; low and sparse, then absent, in the distal ileum.
- **Lymphoid tissue**: **Peyer's patches** are prominent in the ileum, on the antimesenteric border.

**Function.** The jejunum does most bulk absorption of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids. The terminal ileum specializes in absorbing **vitamin B12-intrinsic factor complex** (via the cubilin receptor) and **conjugated bile salts** (via the apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter, ASBT), returning bile acids to the liver in the **enterohepatic circulation**.
levels.phd:
**Developmental origin.** The jejunum and ileum derive from the **midgut**, supplied by the SMA, the artery of the midgut. During week 6 the rapidly elongating midgut loop herniates physiologically into the umbilical cord. It rotates 270 degrees counterclockwise (viewed from the front) around the SMA axis and returns to the abdomen by about week 10 to 11. The cranial limb becomes most of the jejunum and ileum. The caudal limb gives the distal ileum, cecum and proximal colon. The **vitelline duct** joins the loop apex to the yolk sac. If it persists, it forms a **Meckel's diverticulum** on the antimesenteric border of the ileum, about 60 cm (2 feet) from the ileocecal valve. Normal rotation produces the long oblique mesenteric root, which resists twisting.

**Mucosal architecture and gradients.** Surface area is increased in three steps: plicae circulares (valves of Kerckring), villi, and microvilli. Villus height and plica density fall from proximal to distal, while goblet cells, Paneth cells and organized lymphoid follicles increase toward the ileum. **Microfold (M) cells** over Peyer's patches sample luminal antigen for gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT). Enteroendocrine cells also follow a gradient. Proximal I and K cells release CCK and GIP. Distal **L cells** release GLP-1 and PYY, which drive the "ileal brake" that slows gastric emptying when nutrients reach the ileum.

**The mesentery reconsidered.** Classical anatomy described several separate mesenteries. Coffey and O'Leary's work (published 2016 onward) argued that the small bowel mesentery and mesocolon form one **continuous mesenteric organ**, folded and fused to the posterior wall through **Toldt's fascia**. The mesenteric model is now widely accepted in surgical anatomy, but calling the mesentery an "organ" is still partly a matter of definition.

**Vascular pattern.** About 12 to 20 jejunal and ileal branches arise from the left side of the SMA. They form arcades, and terminal **vasa recta** pass to the gut wall without anastomosing with each other. This makes the antimesenteric border the most poorly perfused zone. Lymph drains through lacteals carrying chylomicrons into mesenteric nodes, then the intestinal trunk and the cisterna chyli. This is why dietary fat absorption depends on intact mesenteric lymphatics.
levels.expert:
**Intraoperative orientation.** At laparotomy you cannot see the length directly, so surgeons orient by palpation and transillumination. You can "run the bowel" from the ligament of Treitz to the ileocecal valve, measuring segments for the operative note. Holding a loop to the light shows the vasa recta and arcade pattern: long vasa with clear windows mean proximal bowel, while dense fat and stacked arcades mean distal bowel. To find which way a loop runs, follow the mesentery to its root. The root slopes from upper left to lower right, so tension on a loop shows its proximal end.

**Clinical anatomy of the mesentery:**
- **Volvulus with malrotation**: a narrow-based mesentery tethered by Ladd's bands can twist around the SMA. The result is midgut ischemia, a neonatal surgical emergency. Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation until proven otherwise. On ultrasound or CT, the SMV twisting around the SMA gives a "whirlpool sign." An SMV lying to the left of the SMA suggests malrotation.
- **Internal hernias**: defects in the mesentery, and paraduodenal fossae near the DJ flexure, can trap loops. Mesenteric defects created by Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, especially Petersen's space, are a modern cause of closed-loop obstruction. Surgeons now routinely close these defects.
- **Crohn's disease**: "creeping fat" wraps around the bowel from the mesentery. Crohn's often affects the terminal ileum. Evidence now suggests mesenteric fat and lymphatics drive the disease rather than being bystanders. A trial by Coffey's group found that including the mesentery in ileocolic resection lowered surgical recurrence, but this has not yet become standard everywhere.

**Resection physiology.** Whether a patient copes with resection depends on what remains, not just how much. Losing the jejunum is better tolerated because the ileum can adapt. Losing more than about 100 cm of terminal ileum causes bile acid loss, fat malabsorption, steatorrhea and B12 deficiency. Losing the ileocecal valve speeds transit and allows bacterial overgrowth. **Short bowel syndrome** is generally defined as less than about 200 cm of remaining small bowel. Intestinal adaptation can be enhanced with **teduglutide**, a GLP-2 analogue.

**Meckel's pitfalls.** Meckel's diverticulum may contain heterotopic gastric mucosa, which causes painless bleeding in children. It shows up on technetium-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy. It can also act as a lead point for intussusception, or mimic appendicitis.

**Open questions** include the mesentery's role in the spread of malignancy, its role as an endocrine and immune organ, and how to measure bowel length reliably in vivo, since measurements vary with tone and technique.

keyPoints: Jejunum (proximal ~2/5) and ileum (distal ~3/5) run from the DJ flexure to the ileocecal junction
Jejunum: wider, redder, thicker, tall plicae, long vasa recta, few arcades, little fat
Ileum: paler, more arcade tiers, short vasa recta, more fat, Peyer's patches
Mesentery root (~15 cm) runs from L2 left of midline to the right sacroiliac joint
Terminal ileum absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts (enterohepatic circulation)
Meckel's diverticulum: vitelline duct remnant on the ileum, about 60 cm from the ileocecal valve

test.q: Which feature best identifies a loop as jejunum rather than ileum?
choices: Abundant fat reaching the gut wall
Prominent Peyer's patches in the wall
Many tiers of small arterial arcades
Long vasa recta with few arcades
test.explain: The jejunum has long vasa recta and only one or two arcades. The other three options describe ileum.

test.q: The root of the mesentery runs from the duodenojejunal flexure toward which landmark?
test.explain: The roughly 15 cm root runs obliquely from left of L2 down to the right sacroiliac joint.

test.q: Which nutrient is absorbed mainly in the terminal ileum?
test.explain: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor is absorbed by cubilin receptors in the terminal ileum. Non-heme iron and calcium are absorbed mostly in the duodenum. Glucose is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and jejunum.

test.q: Which structure is crossed by the root of the mesentery?
choices: Left ureter at the pelvic brim
Tail of the pancreas at the spleen
Left renal vein near the aorta
test.explain: The root crosses the third part of the duodenum, the aorta, the IVC, the right ureter and the right psoas.

test.q: The artery supplying the jejunum and ileum is the:
test.explain: The SMA is the artery of the midgut, and the jejunum and ileum are midgut structures.

test.q: What is the ligament of Treitz also called?
test.explain: It suspends the duodenojejunal flexure, which marks where the jejunum begins.

test.q: Compared with the jejunum, the ileum's mucosal folds are:
test.explain: Plicae circulares get shorter and fewer toward the distal ileum, where they disappear.

test.q: Why does the jejunum look redder than the ileum?
test.explain: The jejunum has a richer blood supply. Its wall is actually thicker than the ileum's, not thinner.

test.q: In what general region does most of the ileum lie?
choices: Right upper quadrant near the liver
test.explain: The jejunum sits mostly upper left, and the ileum lies mostly lower right and in the pelvis.

test.q: Lymphoid aggregates on the antimesenteric wall of the ileum are called ___ patches.
test.explain: Peyer's patches are organized gut-associated lymphoid tissue, most prominent in the ileum.

test.q: What is the name of the inner circular folds of the small intestine (Latin term)?
test.explain: Plicae circulares, also called valves of Kerckring, increase the absorptive surface area.

test.q: What is the name of the double fold of peritoneum that suspends the jejunum and ileum?
test.explain: The mesentery carries vessels, lymphatics and nerves between its two layers.

kidTest.q: What does the small intestine mostly do?
choices: Soaks food up into the blood
kidTest.explain: Most food is absorbed in the small intestine.

kidTest.q: Which part is wide, red and busy?
kidTest.explain: The jejunum is the wide, red, busy part.

kidTest.q: Which part soaks up vitamin B12?
kidTest.explain: The ileum, the last part, absorbs vitamin B12.

kidTest.q: What does the mesentery do?
kidTest.explain: The fan-shaped mesentery holds the intestine and carries its blood vessels.

kidTest.q: The fan that holds the intestine is the m _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The mesentery works like a curtain holding onto its rod.

advancedTest.q: Why is the antimesenteric border the most vulnerable part of the bowel wall to ischemia?
choices: Venous drainage there passes straight to the systemic veins
Vasa recta are end arteries that do not join each other in the wall
Peyer's patches there compress the submucosal arteries
Arcades end at the mesenteric border in the distal ileum
advancedTest.explain: Vasa recta do not anastomose with each other, so the border farthest from the mesentery is the least perfused.

advancedTest.q: Which resection is most likely to cause steatorrhea and B12 deficiency?
choices: A long segment of terminal ileum
A long segment of proximal jejunum
advancedTest.explain: The terminal ileum reclaims bile salts and absorbs B12. Losing it causes bile acid loss, fat malabsorption and B12 deficiency, which the jejunum cannot take over.

advancedTest.q: Why is a narrow-based mesentery in malrotation dangerous?
choices: It forces the SMV to drain into the IVC
It allows the midgut to twist around the SMA axis
It brings the ileum up next to the stomach
It stops lymph from reaching the cisterna chyli
advancedTest.explain: Normal rotation creates a long oblique root that resists twisting. A narrow pedicle allows volvulus around the SMA, causing midgut ischemia.

advancedTest.q: A child has painless bleeding and a positive technetium-99m pertechnetate scan. The best explanation is:
choices: Gastric-type mucosa in a vitelline remnant
Ileal Crohn's disease with creeping fat
Bleeding from an internal mesenteric hernia
A Peyer's patch acting as a lead point
advancedTest.explain: Pertechnetate is taken up by gastric mucosa. Heterotopic gastric mucosa in a Meckel's diverticulum causes ulceration and bleeding.

lessons.title: Colon, Cecum and the Appendix

levels.kid:
Your large intestine is like a big upside-down letter U around your tummy. Food that your small intestine has finished with comes in at the bottom right corner.

That corner is a pouch called the **cecum**. Hanging off it is a tiny tube, about as long as your finger, called the **appendix**. Sometimes it gets blocked and swollen. That is called appendicitis, and doctors may need to take it out.

Then the large intestine goes up, across the top, and down the left side. Its job is to soak water back into your body, like squeezing a wet sponge. What is left becomes poop.

The outside has three stripes of muscle that scrunch it into little pockets, like a caterpillar.
levels.hs:
The **large intestine** runs about 1.5 metres from the end of the small intestine to the anus. Its main jobs are absorbing water and salts and storing waste.

Its parts, in order:
- **Cecum**: a blind-ended pouch in the lower right abdomen, where the ileum enters through the **ileocecal valve**.
- **Appendix**: a narrow worm-shaped tube attached to the cecum. It contains lots of lymphoid (immune) tissue.
- **Ascending colon**, going up the right side.
- **Transverse colon**, crossing the top of the abdomen.
- **Descending colon**, going down the left side.
- **Sigmoid colon**, an S-shaped loop leading to the rectum.

The colon looks different from the small intestine. Its outer muscle is gathered into three ribbons called **taeniae coli**. Because they are shorter than the tube, the wall bunches into pouches called **haustra**. Small fat tags called **epiploic appendages** hang off the surface.

A real example: **appendicitis**. Pain often starts vaguely around the belly button, then moves to the lower right abdomen near **McBurney's point**. It sits one-third of the way from the bony bump at the front of the hip to the navel. This is one of the most common reasons for emergency abdominal surgery.
levels.college:
**Distinguishing features.** The colon is wider than the small bowel and has three diagnostic surface features:
- **Taeniae coli**: three longitudinal muscle bands (mesocolic, omental, free). They converge at the base of the appendix, which is how surgeons find it.
- **Haustra**: sacculations produced because the taeniae are shorter than the wall.
- **Omental (epiploic) appendices**: fat-filled peritoneal tags.
The rectum has none of these. There the taeniae spread into a continuous longitudinal layer.

**Peritoneal relations.**
- Intraperitoneal, with a mesentery: transverse colon (transverse mesocolon) and sigmoid colon (sigmoid mesocolon). The appendix has its own small mesoappendix.
- Secondarily retroperitoneal: ascending and descending colon, fused to the posterior wall. Lateral to them lie the **paracolic gutters**.
- The cecum is usually intraperitoneal but has no true mesentery.
- Flexures: the **hepatic (right colic) flexure** and the higher **splenic (left colic) flexure**. The splenic flexure is anchored by the phrenicocolic ligament.

**Cecum and appendix.** The ileum enters the cecum at the **ileocecal valve** (ileal papilla). The appendiceal orifice lies about 2 cm below it. The appendix averages about 6 to 10 cm. Its base is fixed, but its tip varies:
- retrocecal: the most common position
- pelvic: also common
- subcecal, or pre- or postileal

Tip position changes the symptoms. A retrocecal appendix may irritate the psoas, giving a positive **psoas sign**. A pelvic one may irritate the obturator internus, giving the **obturator sign**, or the bladder and rectum.

**Blood supply in brief.** The cecum, appendix, ascending colon and proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon are midgut. They are supplied by SMA branches: ileocolic, appendicular, right colic and middle colic. The distal third onward is hindgut, supplied by the IMA: left colic and sigmoid arteries. The **marginal artery** links the two systems along the colon's inner border.

**Function.** The colon absorbs water and electrolytes, ferments fibre into short-chain fatty acids, and moves contents by segmental and mass movements.
levels.phd:
**Embryology explains the adult layout.** The midgut loop herniates into the umbilical cord around week 6. It returns around week 10 after a total 270° counterclockwise rotation, viewed from the front, around the SMA axis. The cecal bud is the last part to return. It descends from a subhepatic position to the right iliac fossa. Several errors follow from this sequence:
- Incomplete descent leaves a **subhepatic cecum and appendix**.
- Malrotation can produce **Ladd bands** and midgut volvulus.
- Failure of the mesentery to fuse leaves a **mobile cecum**, which predisposes to cecal volvulus.
The ascending and descending mesocolons normally fuse with the posterior parietal peritoneum to form the avascular **fusion fascia of Toldt**. This is the plane developed in medial-to-lateral and lateral-to-medial colectomy.

**The midgut-hindgut junction.** This junction lies at the distal third of the transverse colon. Here SMA and IMA territories meet, along with vagal and pelvic splanchnic parasympathetic supply. The colon's smooth muscle has a special arrangement. Taeniae are thickened longitudinal muscle, while the circular layer is continuous. Interstitial cells of Cajal generate slow waves, and high-amplitude propagated contractions underlie mass movements.

**The appendix.**
- Wall: dense submucosal lymphoid follicles that peak in adolescence, matching the age peak of appendicitis.
- The appendicular artery, from the ileocolic artery, is an **end artery**. Obstruction and rising luminal pressure therefore cause venous congestion, ischaemia, then gangrene and perforation.
- Causes of obstruction include faecolith and lymphoid hyperplasia. The classic obstruction theory explains only some cases.
- Immune role: the **biofilm/safe-house hypothesis** (Bollinger, Parker and colleagues, 2007) proposes that it reseeds commensal flora after diarrhoeal illness. This is supported by its repeated independent evolution across mammals.
- Epidemiology: some studies associate prior appendectomy with modestly higher *C. difficile* recurrence. It is also associated with lower ulcerative colitis risk, and possibly with Parkinson's disease via α-synuclein in appendiceal tissue. These links are contested.

**Pain migration.** Early visceral distension sends signals through afferents travelling with sympathetic fibres to about T10. This produces periumbilical pain. Spread of inflammation to the parietal peritoneum, innervated somatically, localizes the pain to the right iliac fossa.
levels.expert:
**Diagnosis and imaging.**
- Clinical scores such as Alvarado and the Appendicitis Inflammatory Response score help triage, but none replaces imaging in equivocal cases.
- In children and pregnancy, ultrasound comes first. Signs include a non-compressible appendix over about 6 mm in diameter and periappendiceal fat echogenicity. MRI is the second line, avoiding radiation.
- CT is highly accurate in adults. A pitfall is a retrocecal or pelvic appendix mimicking ureteric colic, pyelonephritis or adnexal pathology.
- In pregnancy the appendix is displaced cranially as the uterus enlarges. Pain is therefore often not at McBurney's point.

**Antibiotics versus surgery.** The CODA trial (2020) found antibiotics non-inferior to appendectomy for general health status in uncomplicated appendicitis. However, about 3 in 10 patients needed appendectomy within 90 days, and appendicolith predicted failure. APPAC follow-up showed recurrence approaching 40% at 5 years. Laparoscopic appendectomy remains standard in many centres. Shared decision-making is now expected.

**Hidden pathology.** Appendiceal neoplasms are found in roughly 1% of specimens, more often over age 40. Examples include neuroendocrine tumours and low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasms, which can cause pseudomyxoma peritonei. This is one argument for interval imaging or colonoscopy after nonoperative care in older adults.

**Colonic surgery.**
- **Complete mesocolic excision** (Hohenberger, 2009): sharp dissection in Toldt's plane with central vascular ligation. It removes more lymph nodes and may improve oncologic outcomes. Trade-offs include risk to the superior mesenteric vein and Henle's gastrocolic trunk.
- **Splenic flexure mobilization** risks splenic capsular tears via omental adhesions.
- **Left colon dissection** endangers the left ureter and gonadal vessels.
- The **cecum** has the largest diameter, so by Laplace's law it reaches the highest wall tension. It is the usual perforation site in distal obstruction with a competent ileocecal valve (closed loop) and in Ogilvie syndrome. A diameter around 12 cm is a commonly cited danger threshold.
- **Volvulus**: sigmoid volvulus is typically managed first by endoscopic detorsion, while cecal volvulus generally needs surgery.

**Open questions.** Open questions include the immunological cost of appendectomy, the colonic microbiome's role in appendicitis, and the role of right- versus left-sided tumour biology. Right-sided colon cancers are more often MSI-high and BRAF-mutant, reflecting different embryologic origin.

keyPoints: Large intestine: cecum, appendix, ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid colon, then rectum
Taeniae coli, haustra and epiploic appendages identify the colon
The three taeniae converge on the base of the appendix
Ascending and descending colon are secondarily retroperitoneal; transverse and sigmoid have mesocolons
Retrocecal is the most common appendix position; McBurney's point marks its surface base
Appendicitis pain migrates from periumbilical (visceral, T10) to right iliac fossa (parietal)

test.q: Which feature helps a surgeon locate the appendix at operation?
choices: Taeniae coli converge at its base
Epiploic appendages cluster at its tip
The ileocecal valve lies beneath its tip
test.explain: The three taeniae coli converge at the appendix base, so following them leads to it.

test.q: Which colon segment is secondarily retroperitoneal?
test.explain: The ascending and descending colon fuse to the posterior wall. The transverse and sigmoid colon keep mesocolons, and the appendix has a mesoappendix.

test.q: What is the most common position of the appendix tip?
test.explain: Retrocecal is the most common position. Pelvic is also common, while a subhepatic position reflects failed cecal descent.

test.q: Haustra are formed because:
choices: The mesocolon folds the wall into pockets
Fat tags pull outward on the colonic wall
The circular muscle is absent in the colon
Taeniae are shorter than the colonic wall
test.explain: The shorter longitudinal bands gather the wall into sacculations.

test.q: Early appendicitis pain is periumbilical mainly because:
choices: Visceral afferents enter the cord around T10
The parietal peritoneum is inflamed early on
The appendix lies directly beneath the umbilicus
The obturator nerve is irritated by the swelling
test.explain: Visceral afferents refer pain to the T10 dermatome around the navel. Later, parietal irritation localizes the pain to the right iliac fossa.

test.q: Which artery supplies the appendix?
test.explain: The appendicular artery, usually a branch of the ileocolic artery, supplies the appendix.

test.q: Where does the midgut give way to the hindgut in the colon?
choices: Where the ileum enters the cecum
Where the hepatic flexure turns medially
Where the sigmoid colon meets the rectum
test.explain: The proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon is midgut (SMA). The distal third onward is hindgut (IMA).

test.q: A positive psoas sign suggests the appendix lies in which position?
test.explain: A retrocecal appendix lies on the psoas, so extending the hip stretches the muscle and causes pain.

test.q: Which part of the large bowel lacks taeniae, haustra and epiploic appendages?
test.explain: In the rectum the taeniae spread into a continuous longitudinal layer, so these features disappear.

test.q: The ileum opens into the cecum through the ileocecal ___.
test.explain: The ileocecal valve, also called the ileal papilla, marks the ileocecal junction.

test.q: Name the surface landmark one-third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus.
test.explain: McBurney's point marks the usual surface position of the appendix base.

test.q: The fused, bloodless plane behind the ascending colon is the fascia of ___.
test.explain: Toldt's fusion fascia forms when the mesocolon fuses to the posterior wall. Surgeons dissect along it during colectomy.

kidTest.q: Where is the appendix attached?
kidTest.explain: The appendix hangs off the cecum, the pouch at the start of the large intestine.

kidTest.q: What is a big job of the large intestine?
choices: Soaking water back into the body
kidTest.explain: It squeezes water out of leftover food, like wringing out a sponge.

kidTest.q: Which side of the tummy is the cecum on?
kidTest.explain: The cecum sits in the lower right corner.

kidTest.q: What is it called when the appendix gets blocked and swollen?
kidTest.explain: Appendicitis means a swollen appendix, and doctors may need to remove it.

kidTest.q: The pouch at the start of the large intestine is the c _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The cecum is the pouch where the large intestine begins.

advancedTest.q: Why does appendiceal obstruction progress readily to gangrene?
choices: The appendicular artery is an end artery with no collaterals
Taeniae compress the wall during each mass movement
The mesoappendix drains into the systemic veins
Lymphoid follicles release toxins that clot the arteries
advancedTest.explain: Rising luminal pressure causes congestion and ischaemia. Because the end artery has no collaterals, the wall necroses.

advancedTest.q: In distal colonic obstruction with a competent ileocecal valve, perforation is most likely in the cecum because:
choices: Its blood supply is from the inferior mesenteric artery
It has no taeniae to resist distension
Its largest diameter gives the highest wall tension
Its wall is the thinnest of the whole colon
advancedTest.explain: By Laplace's law, wall tension rises with radius, so the widest segment fails first in a closed loop.

advancedTest.q: A mobile cecum prone to volvulus results most directly from:
choices: Failure of the ascending mesocolon to fuse posteriorly
Early return of the cecal bud before the small bowel
Excess 270° rotation of the midgut loop
advancedTest.explain: Without fusion to form Toldt's fascia, the cecum stays mobile and can twist.

advancedTest.q: In CODA, which feature best predicted failure of antibiotic treatment?
advancedTest.explain: An appendicolith was associated with higher rates of later appendectomy and complications.

lessons.title: Celiac, SMA and IMA Territories and Watershed Areas

levels.kid:
Your gut is a long, twisty tube, and it needs blood to stay alive, just like a garden needs water.

Three big pipes come off the body's main blood pipe, the **aorta**, to water the gut. The first pipe feeds the top part: the stomach, liver and the start of the small intestine. The second pipe feeds the middle part: most of the small intestine and the first half of the big intestine. The third pipe feeds the bottom part: the rest of the big intestine.

Where one pipe's area meets the next, the water is a bit thin, like the far corner of a garden where two sprinklers barely reach. Doctors call these spots **watershed areas**. If blood flow drops, those corners get thirsty first.
levels.hs:
The gut gets its blood from three unpaired arteries that branch off the front of the **abdominal aorta**. Each one supplies the part of the gut that grew from one region of the embryo:

- **Celiac trunk** (at about the level of the T12 vertebra): supplies the **foregut**, which runs from the lower esophagus to the middle of the duodenum. It also feeds the liver, gallbladder, pancreas (partly) and spleen.
- **Superior mesenteric artery (SMA)** (about L1): supplies the **midgut**, which runs from the middle of the duodenum to about two-thirds of the way along the transverse colon.
- **Inferior mesenteric artery (IMA)** (about L3): supplies the **hindgut**, which runs from the last third of the transverse colon to the upper rectum.

Neighboring territories connect through **anastomoses**, which are links between arteries. They act as backup routes. The **marginal artery** runs along the inner edge of the colon and joins SMA and IMA branches.

A **watershed area** is a border zone at the far end of two blood supplies, where flow is weakest. The classic example is the **splenic flexure** of the colon, called **Griffiths' point**. When blood pressure falls, for example in severe blood loss or shock, these zones are the first to suffer **ischemia**, meaning too little blood. That is why **ischemic colitis** often appears at the splenic flexure.
levels.college:
**Celiac trunk (foregut).** It is short and branches into three vessels:
- **Left gastric**: lesser curvature and the esophageal branches.
- **Splenic**: runs tortuously along the upper pancreas and gives short gastrics, the left gastro-omental artery and pancreatic branches.
- **Common hepatic**: gives the gastroduodenal artery (GDA), then continues as the proper hepatic. The GDA gives the right gastro-omental and **superior pancreaticoduodenal** arteries. The right gastric usually arises from the proper hepatic.

**SMA (midgut).** It arises behind the pancreatic neck and passes anterior to the third part of the duodenum and the left renal vein. Branches:
- **Inferior pancreaticoduodenal**, which anastomoses with the superior pancreaticoduodenal. This is the main celiac-SMA link around the pancreatic head.
- **Jejunal and ileal arteries** (from its left side).
- **Ileocolic**, **right colic** (often absent) and **middle colic**.

**IMA (hindgut).** It arises behind the third part of the duodenum. Branches:
- **Left colic**.
- **Sigmoid arteries**.
- **Superior rectal**, its terminal branch. It anastomoses with the middle and inferior rectal arteries from the internal iliac and internal pudendal arteries.

**Collateral routes.**
- **Marginal artery of Drummond**: a continuous arcade along the mesenteric border of the colon.
- **Arc of Riolan** (meandering mesenteric artery): a more central link between the middle colic and left colic arteries.

**Watershed zones.**
- **Griffiths' point** at the splenic flexure, where the marginal artery may be thin or interrupted.
- **Sudeck's point** at the rectosigmoid, between the last sigmoid artery and the superior rectal artery.

These zones are prone to **non-occlusive ischemia** during low blood flow, such as cardiac failure, sepsis or vasopressor use.
levels.phd:
The three-trunk pattern comes from the embryonic **vitelline arteries**. Paired ventral segmental branches fuse into midline vessels, and the longitudinal ventral anastomosis between them regresses. Most regress, leaving only three trunks; persistent links explain variants. The **arc of Bühler** is a remnant of that ventral anastomosis connecting celiac and SMA directly. A **celiacomesenteric trunk** is a common origin of both vessels. A **replaced right hepatic artery** arising from the SMA is the commonest hepatic variant, seen in roughly 10-20% of people in Michels' classic dissections. A replaced left hepatic artery from the left gastric is also common.

The watershed concept reflects how the **resistance network** is built. Flow across a collateral depends on the pressure gradient and on the vessel radius to the fourth power (Poiseuille). When both feeding territories are well perfused, there is little gradient across Griffiths' point, so collaterals stay small. Studies of the marginal artery report that it is attenuated or discontinuous at the splenic flexure in a notable minority of people, although estimates vary widely. The existence of a true "critical point" at Sudeck's point is contested. Modern surgical series suggest rectosigmoid ischemia after high IMA ligation is uncommon when the marginal arcade is intact.

Inside the bowel wall, **vasa recta** are end arteries to the antimesenteric border. This makes the antimesenteric edge relatively vulnerable. Mucosal villus tips are also at risk because of countercurrent oxygen exchange between arteriole and venule, so the mucosa is injured first and the muscularis later.

Splanchnic flow is about 20-25% of cardiac output at rest. It is regulated by **sympathetic α1-mediated vasoconstriction** and by **angiotensin II and vasopressin**, which constrict mesenteric vessels strongly. Shock therefore deliberately shunts blood away from the gut, and this underlies non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia (**NOMI**). Gradual atherosclerotic occlusion is usually tolerated until two of the three trunks are involved, because collaterals enlarge over time (arteriogenesis). This explains why chronic mesenteric ischemia classically requires multivessel disease.
levels.expert:
Clinical consequences follow the territory and the time course.

**Acute mesenteric ischemia.**
- **Embolic occlusion**, usually from atrial fibrillation, lodges a few centimetres beyond the SMA origin, often past the middle colic artery. The proximal jejunum and transverse colon may therefore be spared.
- **Thrombosis** at a stenotic ostium involves the whole SMA territory from the proximal jejunum onward.
- The hallmark is pain out of proportion to the examination.
- **CT angiography** is the diagnostic standard. Lactate is insensitive early.
- Treatment includes revascularisation (open embolectomy, or endovascular approaches including retrograde open mesenteric stenting) with assessment of bowel viability. Planned second-look laparotomy is common.

**Ischemic colitis.** This is the commonest gut ischemia and is usually non-occlusive. It favours the left colon and the watershed zones. Isolated right-colon ischemia carries a worse prognosis and should prompt imaging of the SMA.

**Iatrogenic watershed injury.**
- During **open AAA repair** or **EVAR**, the IMA may be covered or ligated. Colonic ischemia then depends on the marginal artery, the arc of Riolan and internal iliac flow. Bilateral internal iliac exclusion increases the risk.
- A large, enlarged arc of Riolan on angiography signals SMA or IMA stenosis. Ligating it can devascularise a whole territory.
- In anterior resection, surgeons debate **high versus low IMA ligation**. The trade-offs are lymph node yield and pedicle reach against perfusion of the anastomosis. **Indocyanine green fluorescence angiography** is increasingly used to assess perfusion before anastomosis, though trial evidence on whether it reduces leaks is mixed.

**Anatomic pitfalls in hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery.**
- A replaced right hepatic artery runs behind the pancreatic head and portal vein. It is at risk in Whipple procedures.
- If the celiac origin is stenosed, flow to the liver may depend on the GDA via pancreaticoduodenal arcades. Ligating the GDA then risks liver and stomach ischemia. Surgeons test this by clamping the GDA before division.

**Compression syndromes.**
- **Median arcuate ligament syndrome**: the diaphragmatic crura compress the celiac origin, worse on expiration. It is controversial as a pain syndrome, and some propose a neurogenic mechanism involving the celiac plexus.
- **SMA syndrome**: a narrowed aortomesenteric angle compresses the third part of the duodenum, typically after rapid weight loss.

Open questions include reliable perfusion biomarkers and how to individualise collateral risk before vascular and colorectal surgery.

keyPoints: Celiac trunk supplies foregut (lower esophagus to mid-duodenum, liver, spleen, pancreas)
SMA supplies midgut (mid-duodenum to proximal two-thirds of transverse colon)
IMA supplies hindgut (distal transverse colon to upper rectum)
Pancreaticoduodenal arcades link celiac and SMA; marginal artery and arc of Riolan link SMA and IMA
Watershed zones: Griffiths' point (splenic flexure) and Sudeck's point (rectosigmoid)
Low-flow states cause non-occlusive ischemia first in watershed zones

test.q: Which artery supplies the midgut?
test.explain: The SMA supplies the gut from the mid-duodenum to the distal third of the transverse colon. The celiac supplies the foregut and the IMA the hindgut.

test.q: The watershed zone at the splenic flexure is called:
test.explain: Griffiths' point lies between the SMA and IMA territories. Sudeck's point is at the rectosigmoid.

test.q: Which is a direct branch of the celiac trunk?
test.explain: The celiac trunk divides into the left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries. The other three options are SMA or IMA branches.

test.q: The main anastomosis between celiac and SMA territories runs around the:
test.explain: The superior pancreaticoduodenal (celiac via the GDA) and inferior pancreaticoduodenal (SMA) arteries form arcades around the pancreatic head.

test.q: Which part of the gut does the IMA supply?
test.explain: The IMA supplies the hindgut: the distal transverse, descending and sigmoid colon and the upper rectum.

test.q: Why are watershed areas vulnerable when blood pressure falls?
choices: They sit at the far ends of two supplies
They are supplied by the aorta directly
test.explain: Border zones are at the end of two arterial supplies, so perfusion there is weakest when flow drops.

test.q: The superior rectal artery is the terminal branch of the:
test.explain: The superior rectal artery continues the IMA. The middle and inferior rectal arteries come from internal iliac branches.

test.q: The SMA passes anterior to which structure?
test.explain: The SMA crosses anterior to the third part of the duodenum and the left renal vein. It arises behind the pancreatic neck, not in front of it.

test.q: Which type of colon ischemia is most common?
test.explain: Ischemic colitis is usually non-occlusive and favors the left colon and the watershed zones.

test.q: The marginal artery of ___ runs along the colon linking SMA and IMA branches.
test.explain: The marginal artery of Drummond is a continuous arcade along the mesenteric border of the colon.

test.q: Which vertebral level is the usual origin of the celiac trunk?
test.explain: The celiac trunk arises at about T12, the SMA at about L1 and the IMA at about L3.

test.q: Too little blood flow to a tissue is called ___.
test.explain: Ischemia means inadequate blood supply. Watershed zones are the first places to show it.

kidTest.q: What is the big main blood pipe that the gut pipes branch from?
kidTest.explain: All three gut arteries come off the aorta.

kidTest.q: How many big pipes water the gut?
kidTest.explain: Three pipes feed the top, middle and bottom parts of the gut.

kidTest.q: Where is a watershed area?
choices: Right at the start of a pipe
kidTest.explain: It's the border spot that both pipes barely reach.

kidTest.q: What happens to watershed areas when blood flow drops?
kidTest.explain: Those far corners get too little blood first.

kidTest.q: The garden helpers that spray water are called s _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The lesson compares watershed areas to garden corners that two sprinklers barely reach.

advancedTest.q: An embolus in the SMA spares the proximal jejunum and transverse colon. The best explanation is that:
choices: The IMA retrogradely supplies the jejunum
Celiac collaterals supply the whole small bowel
The embolus lodged distal to the middle colic origin
Venous congestion protects the proximal segments
advancedTest.explain: Emboli typically lodge a few centimetres beyond the SMA origin, past the middle colic and proximal jejunal branches, so those segments keep their flow.

advancedTest.q: Why is chronic mesenteric ischemia usually symptomatic only with multivessel disease?
choices: The IMA alone supplies most of the gut
Slow occlusion allows collaterals to enlarge
advancedTest.explain: Gradual stenosis creates pressure gradients across arcades, driving arteriogenesis that compensates until two or more trunks fail.

advancedTest.q: Before dividing the GDA in a Whipple, a surgeon test-clamps it. This most directly checks for:
choices: A replaced left hepatic artery from the left gastric
Arc of Riolan dependence of the colon
Celiac stenosis with liver flow via the SMA
Median arcuate compression of the SMA
advancedTest.explain: With celiac stenosis, hepatic flow may run retrogradely from the SMA through pancreaticoduodenal arcades into the GDA. Ligating it would devascularise the liver.

advancedTest.q: Why do collaterals across Griffiths' point often stay small in healthy people?
choices: The splenic artery steals blood away from the region
Vasa recta end arteries block flow across the flexure
Sympathetic tone keeps the marginal artery constricted
Similar pressures on both sides drive little flow
advancedTest.explain: Collateral flow and growth depend on a pressure gradient. With both trunks patent, there is little gradient, so the link remains attenuated.

lessons.title: Hepatic Portal System and Portosystemic Anastomoses

levels.kid:
Imagine your tummy and gut are a big factory that soaks up food. All the blood leaving that factory carries food bits, and sometimes germs or junk too.

Before that blood goes back to the heart, it takes a special road straight to the **liver**. That road is the **portal vein**. The liver acts like a checkpoint guard. It stores good stuff, cleans out bad stuff, and then lets the blood go on.

There are also tiny back roads that connect the gut's veins to the body's other veins. Usually they are quiet. But if the liver gets scarred and the main road jams, blood squeezes onto the back roads. They swell up like a traffic jam on little side streets, and that can be dangerous.
levels.hs:
Most veins carry blood straight back to the heart. The **hepatic portal system** is different: it carries blood from one capillary bed to a second capillary bed before it returns to the heart. Blood from the stomach, intestines, pancreas and spleen drains into the **portal vein**, which takes it to the **liver**.

Why? Nutrients absorbed by the gut, plus toxins, bacteria and drugs, reach the liver first. The liver processes them, a step called **first-pass metabolism**. After filtering, blood leaves through the **hepatic veins** into the **inferior vena cava** (IVC) and goes to the heart.

The portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas, where the **superior mesenteric vein** joins the **splenic vein**. The **inferior mesenteric vein** usually empties into the splenic vein.

In a few places, portal veins connect with **systemic veins**, the ordinary veins that drain into the vena cavae. These links are called **portosystemic anastomoses**. Normally they carry little blood.

Real example: in **cirrhosis**, liver scarring blocks flow and raises portal pressure (**portal hypertension**). Blood detours through the anastomoses, which swell into **varices**. Swollen veins at the lower esophagus (**esophageal varices**) can rupture and bleed severely. This makes them a medical emergency.
levels.college:
**Formation and course.** The hepatic portal vein (about 8 cm long) forms posterior to the neck of the pancreas, at roughly L1-L2, from the union of the **superior mesenteric vein (SMV)** and **splenic vein**. The **inferior mesenteric vein (IMV)** typically joins the splenic vein, though it may join the SMV or the confluence. The portal vein ascends behind the first part of the duodenum. It then runs in the free edge of the **hepatoduodenal ligament**, posterior to the bile duct and hepatic artery proper, forming the anterior boundary of the **omental (epiploic) foramen**. At the porta hepatis it divides into right and left branches.

**Tributaries joining the trunk directly:** left and right gastric veins, cystic vein, posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal vein and the **paraumbilical veins** (via the left branch). The portal vein supplies about 75% of hepatic blood flow and roughly half the liver's oxygen. The hepatic artery supplies the rest.

**Valveless system.** Portal veins lack functional valves, so flow can reverse when pressure rises.

**Major portosystemic anastomoses:**
- **Esophageal:** left gastric vein with esophageal veins draining to the azygos system. Gives **esophageal varices**.
- **Rectal (anorectal):** superior rectal vein (to IMV) with middle and inferior rectal veins (to internal iliac and internal pudendal veins). Gives **anorectal varices**, which are distinct from ordinary hemorrhoids.
- **Paraumbilical:** paraumbilical veins in the falciform ligament with superficial epigastric veins of the abdominal wall. Gives **caput medusae**.
- **Retroperitoneal:** colic veins and the bare areas of the colon and liver with lumbar, renal and phrenic veins (veins of Retzius).

**Portal hypertension** is a hepatic venous pressure gradient above 5 mmHg. Causes are classified as prehepatic (portal vein thrombosis), intrahepatic (cirrhosis, schistosomiasis) or posthepatic (Budd-Chiari syndrome, right heart failure). Consequences include varices, **splenomegaly** with hypersplenism, ascites and hepatic encephalopathy.
levels.phd:
**Hemodynamics.** Portal pressure follows Ohm's law: ΔP = Q × R. In cirrhosis, resistance rises from two sources. A fixed component comes from fibrosis, regenerative nodules and sinusoidal capillarization, which means loss of the fenestrations of the liver sinusoidal endothelial cells. A dynamic component (roughly a quarter to a third) comes from contraction of activated **hepatic stellate cells** and intrahepatic endothelial dysfunction, with reduced eNOS-derived nitric oxide and increased endothelin-1 and thromboxane.

Paradoxically, splanchnic arterial **vasodilation**, driven by excess NO, carbon monoxide, glucagon and endocannabinoids, raises portal inflow (Q). This sustains hypertension even after collaterals form. It also produces the hyperdynamic circulation and the effective arterial underfilling that activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, sympathetic tone and ADH. That cascade underlies ascites and hepatorenal physiology.

**Measurement.** The **hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG)** is wedged minus free hepatic venous pressure. It reflects sinusoidal pressure and is accurate for sinusoidal causes but underestimates presinusoidal disease such as schistosomiasis or portal vein thrombosis. Above 5 mmHg is portal hypertension. At or above 10 mmHg is **clinically significant portal hypertension**, which predicts varices and decompensation. At or above 12 mmHg variceal bleeding becomes possible, the threshold established by Garcia-Tsao and colleagues in 1985.

**Collateral biology.** Collaterals form both by reopening embryonic channels and by VEGF- and PDGF-driven **angiogenesis**, not merely passive dilation. Experimental anti-angiogenic therapy reduced collateral formation in animal models. Variceal rupture follows Laplace's law: wall tension = (transmural pressure × radius) / wall thickness. Large, thin-walled varices with red wale signs are therefore at highest risk.

**Anatomical nuance.** The left gastric (coronary) vein carries the esophageal collateral load. **Splenic vein thrombosis** (often from pancreatitis) causes left-sided or sinistral portal hypertension with isolated gastric fundal varices via the short gastric veins, while HVPG stays normal. **Streamlining** within the portal vein, with SMV flow favoring the right lobe and splenic flow the left, was proposed to explain uneven distribution of metastases and abscesses. The evidence for it remains debated.
levels.expert:
**Clinical translation.** Under the Baveno VII consensus (2022), noninvasive tests now often stand in for HVPG. A liver stiffness by transient elastography of at least 25 kPa effectively rules in clinically significant portal hypertension in most etiologies. Stiffness below 20 kPa with a platelet count above 150 × 10⁹/L can spare a patient screening endoscopy. Nonselective beta-blockers, carvedilol in particular, are used to prevent decompensation, not merely first bleeding. This rationale came from the PREDESCI trial. Spleen stiffness is an emerging adjunct.

**Acute variceal hemorrhage.** Management combines restrictive transfusion (overtransfusion raises portal pressure and rebleeding), vasoactive drugs (terlipressin, somatostatin or octreotide), antibiotic prophylaxis and endoscopic band ligation. Gastric fundal varices are often treated with cyanoacrylate injection instead. **Pre-emptive TIPS** within 72 hours in high-risk patients (Child-Pugh C 10-13 or B with active bleeding) improved survival in the trial by Garcia-Pagán and colleagues (2010). Balloon tamponade with a Sengstaken-Blakemore or Minnesota tube is a temporizing bridge.

**TIPS anatomy.** The transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt is a stent placed from a hepatic vein, usually the right, through liver parenchyma into a portal branch, usually the right. It creates an iatrogenic portosystemic anastomosis. Covered PTFE stents have largely replaced bare stents because of better patency. Diverting portal blood away from the liver risks **hepatic encephalopathy** and can unmask cardiac failure. Gastric varices with a **gastrorenal shunt** can instead be closed by BRTO (balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration). Surgical portacaval and distal splenorenal (Warren) shunts are now rare.

**Pitfalls:**
- Anorectal varices are not hemorrhoids. Hemorrhoids are vascular cushions whose prevalence is not increased in portal hypertension. Banding varices as if they were hemorrhoids is dangerous.
- Prominent abdominal wall veins draining upward from below the umbilicus suggest IVC obstruction, not caput medusae.
- Surgeons face hemorrhage from retroperitoneal collaterals during adhesiolysis or stoma formation. Stomal varices are a recognized bleeding source.
- Congenital extrahepatic portosystemic shunts (Abernethy malformation) present with encephalopathy or nodules.

**Neuro link.** Shunted ammonia drives astrocyte glutamine accumulation, swelling and low-grade cerebral edema in encephalopathy. In acute liver failure, intracranial hypertension can become a neurosurgical monitoring problem.

keyPoints: The portal vein forms behind the pancreatic neck from the SMV and splenic vein
Portal blood reaches the liver first, allowing first-pass processing of gut-absorbed substances
The liver gets about 75% of its blood from the portal vein, the rest from the hepatic artery
Key anastomoses: esophageal, anorectal, paraumbilical and retroperitoneal
Portal hypertension (HVPG above 5 mmHg) opens collaterals into varices; bleeding risk starts at 12 mmHg
TIPS creates an artificial portosystemic shunt to decompress the portal system

test.q: Which two veins unite to form the hepatic portal vein?
test.explain: The SMV joins the splenic vein behind the neck of the pancreas. The IMV usually drains into the splenic vein rather than forming the trunk.

test.q: Where does the portal vein form?
test.explain: The confluence lies posterior to the neck of the pancreas. The vein then ascends to the porta hepatis, where it divides.

test.q: Esophageal varices form mainly where which portal vein meets the azygos drainage?
test.explain: The left gastric vein anastomoses with esophageal veins that drain into the azygos system.

test.q: Caput medusae results from enlarged collaterals between paraumbilical veins and:
test.explain: Paraumbilical veins in the falciform ligament connect with superficial abdominal wall veins, such as the superficial epigastric veins, so the dilated veins radiate from the umbilicus.

test.q: Why can blood flow backward in portal tributaries?
choices: They drain into the azygos vein
test.explain: The portal system is essentially valveless, so a rise in pressure can reverse flow toward systemic veins.

test.q: Roughly what share of liver blood flow does the portal vein provide?
test.explain: The portal vein supplies about 75% of flow; the hepatic artery supplies the remainder.

test.q: Which is a posthepatic cause of portal hypertension?
test.explain: Budd-Chiari syndrome obstructs hepatic venous outflow beyond the liver. Portal vein thrombosis is prehepatic; cirrhosis and schistosomiasis are intrahepatic.

test.q: In the hepatoduodenal ligament, the portal vein lies:
test.explain: The portal vein runs posterior to the bile duct and hepatic artery proper, forming the front wall of the omental foramen.

test.q: The anorectal anastomosis links the superior rectal vein with veins that drain to the:
test.explain: The superior rectal vein drains via the inferior mesenteric vein to the portal system. The middle and inferior rectal veins drain to the internal iliac and internal pudendal veins, which are systemic. The anorectal anastomosis therefore links portal and systemic circulation.

test.q: Processing of gut-absorbed substances by the liver before they reach the body is called first-___ metabolism.
test.explain: Portal blood reaches the liver first, so first-pass metabolism happens before systemic circulation.

test.q: What term describes swollen, dilated collateral veins that form in portal hypertension?
test.explain: Varices are dilated collateral veins that can rupture and bleed.

test.q: What is the abbreviation for the stent-created shunt from a hepatic vein to a portal branch?
test.explain: TIPS stands for transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt.

kidTest.q: Where does the portal vein take blood from the gut?
kidTest.explain: The portal vein carries gut blood to the liver first.

kidTest.q: What job does the liver do with gut blood?
kidTest.explain: The liver stores good stuff and cleans out bad stuff.

kidTest.q: What happens when a scarred liver jams the main road?
kidTest.explain: Blood detours through small back roads, which swell up.

kidTest.q: Why are swollen back-road veins a worry?
kidTest.explain: Swollen veins can burst, and that bleeding is dangerous.

kidTest.q: Which organ is the checkpoint guard for gut blood? l _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: The liver checks gut blood before it goes to the heart.

advancedTest.q: A patient with pancreatitis develops isolated gastric fundal varices with a normal HVPG. The best explanation is:
choices: Diffuse cirrhosis raising intrahepatic sinusoidal resistance
Paraumbilical vein recanalization after chronic liver injury
Hepatic vein outflow occlusion as in Budd-Chiari syndrome
Splenic vein thrombosis with short gastric rerouting
advancedTest.explain: Splenic vein thrombosis causes left-sided portal hypertension; splenic blood reroutes through short gastric veins while sinusoidal pressure, and thus HVPG, stays normal.

advancedTest.q: Why does portal hypertension persist after large collaterals have formed?
choices: Hepatic artery flow falls and blocks portal outflow
Collaterals add new resistance in series with the liver
Valves in the portal tributaries close under pressure
advancedTest.explain: By ΔP = Q × R, NO-driven splanchnic vasodilation increases portal inflow, sustaining pressure despite decompressing collaterals.

advancedTest.q: HVPG would most likely underestimate portal pressure in which condition?
advancedTest.explain: HVPG reflects sinusoidal pressure. Schistosomiasis causes presinusoidal obstruction, so wedged pressure misses the true portal pressure.

advancedTest.q: Overtransfusion in acute variceal bleeding is avoided mainly because it:
choices: Raises portal pressure and rebleeding risk
Closes the left gastric collateral channel
Lowers splanchnic flow and causes ischemia
advancedTest.explain: Volume expansion increases portal pressure, which raises variceal wall tension and promotes rebleeding; restrictive transfusion is preferred.

lessons.title: Visceral Innervation, Enteric Plexuses and Referred Pain

levels.kid:
Your gut has its own tiny brain! It is a net of nerve cells inside the wall of your tummy tubes. It squeezes food along like toothpaste in a tube, even while you sleep.

Your big brain sends messages too. One set of nerves says "rest and digest," so the gut works harder. Another set says "run!", so the gut slows down.

Here is a funny trick. When a tummy organ hurts, your brain can get confused about where the pain is. A sore appendix often hurts near your belly button first. A sore heart can make your arm ache. Doctors call this **referred pain**, and they use it like a map to find the problem.
levels.hs:
The gut is controlled by the **autonomic nervous system**, the part of the nervous system you don't consciously control.

- **Parasympathetic** nerves ("rest and digest") speed up gut movement and secretion. The **vagus nerve** supplies the gut from the esophagus to about two-thirds of the way along the transverse colon. After that, **pelvic splanchnic nerves** from spinal levels S2-S4 take over.
- **Sympathetic** nerves ("fight or flight") slow the gut and narrow its blood vessels. They travel in **splanchnic nerves** from the thoracic and lumbar spinal cord.

Inside the gut wall is the **enteric nervous system**, sometimes called the "second brain." It has two nerve networks (plexuses). The **myenteric plexus** controls muscle movement (peristalsis), and the **submucosal plexus** controls secretion and local blood flow. It can run reflexes on its own.

Pain from organs is dull and hard to pinpoint. The brain often maps it onto the skin supplied by the same spinal segments. This is **referred pain**. Example: early **appendicitis** pain is felt around the belly button (the T10 dermatome). Later it moves to the lower right abdomen, once the inflamed appendix irritates the nearby body wall lining, which has precise nerves.
levels.college:
**Sympathetic supply.** Preganglionic fibres leave the cord (T5-L2), pass through the sympathetic trunk without synapsing, and form splanchnic nerves:
- Greater (T5-T9) to the **celiac ganglion**, serving the foregut
- Lesser (T10-T11) to the **superior mesenteric / aorticorenal ganglia**, serving the midgut
- Least (T12) and lumbar splanchnics (L1-L2) to the **inferior mesenteric ganglion**, serving the hindgut

Postganglionic fibres follow the arteries to the organs. Their effects are vasoconstriction, sphincter contraction and reduced motility.

**Parasympathetic supply.** The vagus (anterior and posterior vagal trunks) supplies the foregut and midgut. Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) ascend through the hypogastric plexuses to the hindgut. Their preganglionic fibres synapse on enteric neurons in the gut wall.

**Enteric nervous system.** The ENS contains roughly 200-600 million neurons.
- **Myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus**, between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers, controls motility.
- **Submucosal (Meissner's) plexus** controls secretion, absorption and blood flow.

The peristaltic reflex works like this: stretch above a food bolus causes contraction (acetylcholine, substance P), while the gut below relaxes (VIP, nitric oxide).

**Visceral pain.** The gut is insensitive to cutting but sensitive to stretch, ischaemia and inflammation. Pain afferents travel back with the sympathetic fibres, so pain is referred by embryonic segment:
- Foregut to the epigastrium (T5-T9)
- Midgut to the periumbilical region (T10-T11)
- Hindgut to the suprapubic region (T12-L2)

Once inflammation reaches the **parietal peritoneum**, which has somatic innervation, pain localizes sharply.

Classic referrals:
- Gallbladder pain goes to the epigastrium and right scapula.
- Diaphragmatic irritation goes to the shoulder tip (C3-C5, phrenic nerve).
- Myocardial ischaemia goes to the left arm (T1-T4).
levels.phd:
**Convergence-projection theory.** Referred pain is classically explained by convergence (Ruch, 1940s). Visceral and cutaneous afferents synapse on the same dorsal horn neurons, mainly in laminae I and V. Visceral afferents are sparse, under 10% of spinal afferent input, and each fibre spreads widely across several segments. The brain therefore attributes the activity to the more richly represented somatic field.

This also explains several features of visceral pain:
- Poor localization and bilateral, midline perception, because midline organs have bilateral innervation.
- Secondary somatic hyperalgesia over the referred zone.

Head's zones (1890s) mapped these skin areas, and Mackenzie described the accompanying muscle guarding (viscerosomatic reflexes).

**Afferent pathways.** Spinal visceral afferents have cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia. They are peptidergic (CGRP, substance P) and express TRPV1 and mechanosensitive Piezo2. They mediate nociception. Vagal afferents, with cell bodies in the nodose ganglion projecting to the nucleus tractus solitarius, make up about 80% of vagal fibres. They mainly carry physiological signals such as satiety, nausea and chemosensation.

Pelvic visceral pain follows the **pelvic pain line**. Organs below the peritoneum, such as the sigmoid colon and rectum, send pain via pelvic splanchnic (parasympathetic) afferents to S2-S4. Organs above it send pain with sympathetic fibres.

The visceral afferent fibres themselves are mostly silent at rest. "Silent" nociceptors become active only during inflammation, which underlies peripheral sensitization.

**ENS cell biology.** The ENS derives from vagal and sacral **neural crest**. Migration depends on RET-GDNF signalling and EDNRB-endothelin-3 signalling. Failure of migration in the distal colon causes **Hirschsprung disease**, an aganglionic segment that cannot relax. Intrinsic primary afferent neurons (Dogiel type II) sense the contents of the gut lumen. **Interstitial cells of Cajal** (c-Kit+) generate slow-wave pacemaker activity. Enteric glia, once considered passive support cells, modulate neural signalling and the epithelial barrier.
levels.expert:
**Clinical localization.** Pain migration in appendicitis is the textbook test of these principles. In pelvic or retrocaecal appendicitis, the parietal peritoneum may never be irritated anteriorly. Classic right iliac fossa signs may then be absent, while psoas or obturator signs, or rectal tenderness, appear instead.

Shoulder-tip pain points to diaphragmatic irritation, as in splenic rupture (Kehr sign), a perforated ulcer or laparoscopic CO2. Inferior myocardial infarction presenting as "indigestion" is a recurring diagnostic pitfall.

**Interventional neuroanatomy.** Interrupting the afferent pathways can relieve pain:
- **Celiac plexus neurolysis**, guided by endoscopic ultrasound or CT, palliates pancreatic cancer pain because foregut afferents traverse the celiac ganglia.
- **Superior hypogastric plexus block** treats pelvic cancer pain from organs above the pelvic pain line.
- **Ganglion impar block** treats perineal pain.

Thoracic sympathetic chain injury from surgery or epidural blockade can unmask unopposed vagal tone, producing bowel hyperactivity.

**Surgical nerve preservation.** Total mesorectal excision aims to preserve the hypogastric nerves and pelvic splanchnic nerves, which form the inferior hypogastric plexus. Damage causes bladder, ejaculatory and erectile dysfunction. Spinal cord injury above about T6 risks **autonomic dysreflexia** when the rectum or bladder is distended. Lesions above the sacral cord leave the reflex bowel intact, whereas conus or cauda equina lesions produce a flaccid, areflexic bowel, which matters in neurosurgical counselling.

**Frontiers.** Several areas are under active study:
- **Gut-brain axis.** Enteroendocrine "neuropod" cells synapse directly onto vagal afferents using glutamate. Gut microbes modulate ENS development and serotonin, with about 90% of body serotonin made by enterochromaffin cells.
- **Visceral hypersensitivity.** In irritable bowel syndrome, peripheral sensitization (mast cells, TRPV1) combines with altered central processing.
- **Parkinson disease.** Braak's hypothesis proposes that alpha-synuclein pathology may spread from the ENS to the brain via the vagus. Epidemiology after truncal vagotomy partly supports this, but the idea remains debated.
- **Enteric neural stem cell transplantation** is being explored for Hirschsprung disease.

keyPoints: Vagus supplies gut to about the distal third of the transverse colon; pelvic splanchnics (S2-S4) supply the rest
Thoracic and lumbar splanchnic nerves carry sympathetic fibres to the celiac, superior and inferior mesenteric ganglia
Myenteric plexus controls motility; submucosal plexus controls secretion and blood flow
Visceral pain refers by embryonic origin: foregut epigastric, midgut periumbilical, hindgut suprapubic
Pain localizes sharply once the somatically innervated parietal peritoneum is irritated
Referred pain arises from visceral and somatic afferents converging on shared dorsal horn neurons

test.q: Which nerves give parasympathetic supply to the descending colon?
test.explain: The hindgut gets parasympathetic fibres from S2-S4 pelvic splanchnics. The vagus stops around the distal transverse colon.

test.q: The myenteric plexus mainly regulates:
test.explain: Auerbach's plexus lies between the muscle layers and drives peristalsis. The submucosal plexus handles secretion and blood flow.

test.q: Early appendicitis pain is usually felt in the:
test.explain: The appendix is midgut, whose pain refers to the T10 periumbilical area.

test.q: Why does appendicitis pain later shift to the right lower abdomen?
test.explain: The parietal peritoneum has somatic nerves, so pain becomes sharp and well localized.

test.q: The greater splanchnic nerve synapses mainly in the:
test.explain: Greater splanchnic fibres (T5-T9) synapse in the celiac ganglion, serving the foregut.

test.q: Pain from the stomach (foregut) is typically referred to the:
test.explain: Foregut pain refers to the epigastrium via T5-T9.

test.q: Shoulder-tip pain from diaphragm irritation travels in the:
test.explain: The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) shares segments with shoulder skin.

test.q: Sympathetic stimulation of the gut tends to:
test.explain: Sympathetic activity slows motility, contracts sphincters and constricts vessels.

test.q: The gut wall is most sensitive to:
test.explain: Viscera ignore cutting but respond to distension, ischaemia and inflammation.

test.q: The submucosal plexus is also called ___'s plexus.
test.explain: Meissner's plexus lies in the submucosa.

test.q: What cranial nerve supplies parasympathetic fibres to the foregut and midgut?
test.explain: The vagus nerve (CN X) supplies the gut to about the distal transverse colon.

test.q: Pain felt on skin far from the diseased organ is called ___ pain.
test.explain: Referred pain follows shared spinal segments.

kidTest.q: What does the gut's own nerve net do?
kidTest.explain: It moves food through the tubes, even while you sleep.

kidTest.q: The 'rest and digest' nerves make the gut:
kidTest.explain: Rest-and-digest nerves help digestion.

kidTest.q: Early appendix pain is often felt near the:
kidTest.explain: The brain maps early appendix pain to the belly button area.

kidTest.q: A sore heart can make which body part ache?
kidTest.explain: Heart pain often spreads to the arm.

kidTest.q: Pain felt in the wrong place is called r _ _ _ _ _ _ _ pain.
kidTest.explain: Referred pain helps doctors find the real problem.

advancedTest.q: Why is visceral pain poorly localized while referred to skin?
choices: Visceral receptors respond to cutting, so the signal is diffuse and weak
Visceral afferents bypass the spinal cord and enter the brainstem directly
Enteric neurons filter ascending signals heavily before they reach the cord
Visceral afferents are sparse and converge on dorsal horn neurons shared with skin
advancedTest.explain: Sparse, widely spreading visceral input converges with dense cutaneous input, so the brain attributes it to skin.

advancedTest.q: Rectal cancer pain is poorly relieved by a superior hypogastric block. Best explanation?
choices: Rectal pain travels mainly in vagal afferents to the nodose ganglion
The rectum lacks sensory innervation and pain arises from nearby skin
Below the pelvic pain line, pain travels in S2-S4 pelvic splanchnic afferents
The superior hypogastric plexus carries mainly motor fibres to the bladder
advancedTest.explain: Organs below the pelvic pain line send pain with parasympathetic fibres to the sacral cord, bypassing that plexus.

advancedTest.q: In Hirschsprung disease, the aganglionic segment is narrowed because:
choices: Sympathetic ganglia overgrow and constrict the bowel wall
Absent inhibitory enteric neurons prevent the bowel from relaxing
Interstitial cells of Cajal overproduce slow waves in the colon
Vagal fibres fail to reach the distal colon during development
advancedTest.explain: Failed neural crest migration removes enteric neurons, including inhibitory (NO, VIP) ones, so the segment stays contracted.

advancedTest.q: Celiac plexus neurolysis helps pancreatic cancer pain mainly because:
choices: It cuts vagal efferents that drive pancreatic secretion
Foregut nociceptive afferents travel through the celiac ganglia
It devascularizes the tumour by blocking the celiac trunk
Pancreatic pain is carried by the phrenic nerve near the celiac axis
advancedTest.explain: Spinal visceral pain afferents run with sympathetic fibres through the celiac plexus, so blocking it interrupts them.
